newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Sundays - May 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Sundays - May 4.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- BT AND BSKYB TO GO INTERACTIVE

BT and BskyB are set to announce plans for a revolutionary interactive television system which will revolutionise the information industry and home entertainment. Oftel is thought to have given an informal go-ahead for the formation of British Interactive Broadcasting which will take advantage of new digital television services. Matsushita and Midland Bank are also involved in the 500m stg joint venture.
-- RATES TO RISE IN ADVANCE OF RADICAL BUDGET

The incoming Chancellor Gordon Brown is set to raise interest rates this week amid concerns that consumer spending and poor expert performance is upsetting the British economy. There is growing speculation that this summer's budget, which will include a windfall tax on privatised utilities and a reduction in VAT on domestic fuel, will prove more radical than previously expected.
-- MASTERCARD FACES SUIT OVER LOLA COLLAPSE

Lola Formula One's liquidator may take legal action over Mastercard International's failure to provide up to 10m dollars in sponsorship. By the time of Lola's collapse, with debts of up to 6m stg, Mastercard had not paid anything. The financial crisis could affect Lola's sister company, Lola Cars, one of the leading chassis manufacturers for F1 and US Indy Car racing.
-- HAMBROS FACES GALILEO ACTION

Liquidator Jason Elles of accountant Ernst & Young is considering suing the merchant bank Hambros over the quality of advice given to Andrew Regan's Galileo group in its failed attempt to take-over the Co-operative Wholesale Society. The High Court revealed that Hambros copied confidential documents and circulated them to more than a dozen City institutions.
-- RJB THREATENS FOUR PIT CLOSURES

Britain's leading coal producer RJB Mining may have to close four of its 19 pits if power generators reduce their purchases significantly when existing contracts run out next year. PowerGen recently signed contracts with Midlands Mining and Mining Scotland for up to 5m tonnes of coal.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- GORDON BROWN'S RATE DILEMMA

A group of leading British exporters, thought to have the backing of the CBI, will lobby the incoming Chancellor to tighten fiscal policy to suppress sterling's strength instead of the widely expected move of raising interest rates. British Steel recently accelerating its job cutting programme because of the strength of the pound particularly in Germany.
-- CHEAP BEER UNDER BLAIR?

Stuart Neame, vice chairman of independent brewer Shepherd Neame, claimed that the Labour Party's Dawn Primarolo has recently promised an inquiry into duty on beer, in a bid to halt soaring duty-free imports from the Continent. A report prepared by Oxford Economic Forecasting on behalf of the Brewers and Licensed Retailers Association called for a 20 per cent cut in duty on beer.
-- LABOUR LOOKS TO BP CHIEF TO BOOST EURO RELATIONS

BP's chairman Sir David Simon is likely to accept an invitation by PM Tony Blair to become the new minister for Europe, and shape the UK's relationship with the rest of its European partners, if he can continue as chairman of BP. Sir David is well known for his pro-European views and would support European Monetary Union under the right circumstances.
-- CITY SEEKS HARD INFLATION STANCE

The Chancellor Gordon Brown is under pressure to demonstrate his toughness on inflation and raise interest rates after Wednesday's meeting with the governor of the Bank of England. The new Labour government is thought to want to pursue a tight monetary policy to build its market credibility.
-- SEARS TO NET 700,000 STG

David James, brought in by Sears to bring under control increasing losses in its high street shoe business, is likely to earn more than 700,000 stg for his one year contract. Mr James will devote half his week to the company to try and reorganising or sell the shoe operation.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- BLAIR FACES EUROPEAN BATTLE TO WIN TOYOTA DEAL

The Japanese motor giant Toyota wants 100m stg in aid from the new Labour government to build a third model at its Derby factory. Britain faces tough competition from France, which may already have offered a generous aid package, and Poland, which is not subject to European Union regulations.
-- BROWN SET TO ORDER RATE RISE

Gordon Brown is set to raise interest rates by a quarter- point this week after meeting the Bank of England governor. The summer budget is unlikely to include radical tax proposals apart from a windfall tax on the privatised utilities.
-- LEGAL THREAT TO REGAN'S BANKERS

Ernst & Young, liquidator to Andrew Regan's Galileo, is considering suing the merchant bank Hambros and law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite over their behaviour in the failed attempt to take-over the Co-operative Wholesale Society. Pressure is growing for action against Hambros corporate financiers who were aware than Regan had illicitly obtained CWS documents.
-- IONICA LINES UP DUAL FLOAT

Fast growing telecommunications group Ionica has appointed SBC Warburg and ABN Amro Hoare Govett as it prepares for dual listing this summer on the London Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. The company needs extra capital to expand despite raising funds in America two months ago.
-- MARCO COOKS UP DEAL WITH GRANADA

Celebrity chef Marco Pierre White has been asked by Granada chairman Gerry Robinson to run the group's restaurants at prestigious London hotels, including the Waldorf and the Meridien. The aim would be to merge the operations with Marco Pierre White's existing restaurants and eventually float the concern as a separate company on the Stock Exchange.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- WORDS OF WISDOM AS BROWN FACES AN ECONOMIC DILEMMA

Gordon Brown will be under pressure from the Bank of England's governor Eddie George to raise interest rates this week to curb inflation. However, economic advisers to the former Chancellor Kenneth Clarke have called for a tightening of fiscal policy, including 2p on income tax and VAT on food and children's clothes, instead of higher interest rates which would hit exports.
-- NEW WARNING IN CO-OP SCANDAL

Liquidator Ernst & Young is considering legal action against City bank Hambros and law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite for its part in the failed attempt by businessman Andrew Regan to take- over the Co-operative Wholesale Society. Mr Justice Lightman had denounced Regan's dishonest conduct last month in a High Court hearing after he obtained confidential Co-op documents.
-- LLOYD'S DOOR SHUTS FOR AN EX-MINISTER

Despite speculation, former president of the Board of Trade Ian Lang is unlikely to be on the short-list of candidates drawn up by headhunter Spencer Stuart for chairmanship of the Lloyd's insurance market. His appointment would have provoked a row amongst Names who were angry that Lang did not step in to help after the market was hit by losses of up to 8bn stg. Former merchant banker Jonathan Agnew is favourite for the job of chairman.
-- SIB FACING AXE BEFORE YEAR END

The Labour government plans to push through amendments to the Financial Services Act to create a new super regulator in the City which would mean the end for the existing Securities and Investments Board. The new administration also want to quickly clear up the review into the mis-selling of pensions.
-- GRANADA BEATS ITS 1.3BN STG SALES DEADLINE
Granada's chairman Gerry Robinson has eased market fears over the company's debt and raised 1.3bn stg of capital ahead of schedule with the sale of 7.5m stg German TV rentals Telerent.
The biggest single deal was the sale of the Welcome Break motorway services chain to Investcorp fro 476m stg.
THE OBSERVER
-- HUGE UPHEAVALS IN PROSPECT AT LLOYD'S

A draft report by Lloyd's of London will call for an end to self-regulation and new legislation to make it answerable to the Securities and Investments Board, the City's key regulator. Few people had expected the review by Sir Alan Hardcastle to concede self-regulation despite his hints at profound changes after recent losses and criticism of the corporation.
-- OUSTED MORGAN FIVE GIVEN CASH TO FIGHT IMRO CHARGES

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell offered financial support to five former executives, in their severance packages, in the event of disciplinary action by unit trust industry regulator Imro. The five executives, including the chief executive of Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, were sacked for failing to prevent the huge losses which took place during the Peter Young scandal.
-- NEW WHITBREAD BOSS PLANS MORE PUB SALES

400 underperforming pubs and 80 off-licences could be axed by Whitbread's new chief executive David Thomas in a bid to streamline the company and improve the group's return on capital. The group has been criticised for paying too much for David Lloyd Leisure and the Pelican Group.
-- 'DOUBLE COUNCIL TAX FOR LARGE HOUSES', SAYS CONTENDER FOR BROWN'S PANEL

John Muellbauer of Nuffield College, Oxford, and widely tipped to be on Gordon Brown's planned council of economic advisers, has called for huge council tax increases for people living in expensive houses. He argues that the current banding system should be abolished to stabilise house prices.
-- CONCERNS OVER REGAN DID NOT DETER HAMBROS

Merchant bank Hambros were humiliated into making a public apology to the Co-operative Wholesale Society after being implicated in a dishonest bid by Andrew Regan's Galileo group to acquire the company. Adviser Peter Young has been suspended while an internal inquiry takes place.
